extracted.intended_audience: Scholars and students in linguistics, pragmatics, and humor research (internet-mediated humor)
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and evaluative standards for researching and interpreting internet-mediated humor using pragmatic (particularly Relevance Theory) and multimodal approaches. Targets the conduct, presentation, and theoretical framing of academic studies of online humor (memes, social media, messaging).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical grounding in Relevance Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit Relevance Theory (RT) from cognitive pragmatics to account for how people make sense of humorous discourse and to highlight differences between humorous and non-humorous communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 2 provides a detailed presentation of RT concepts (communicative/informative intentions, anticipatory/backwards inferencing, search for relevance, dynamic context, explicatures/implicatures) and uses RT to account for incongruity-resolution. The reviewer notes these analytical tools are suitable for detecting subtle cognitive mechanisms of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary enrichment
rubrics_metrics.description: Enrich humor-research concepts and tools with approaches originating in adjacent areas beyond core humor studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer emphasizes importance of combining theoretical concepts from humor research with those from related fields (cognitive pragmatics, cyberpragmatics) to better explain internet-mediated humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit attention to contextual particularities of internet humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into consideration the contextual particularities of internet humor (new participant types, hybrid/collaborative discourse, new interfaces, multiplicity of interpretations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Introduction promises context-specific treatment throughout the study; internet context includes asynchronous/asynchronous interaction, textual/visual affordances, and heterogeneous audiences (context collapse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize internet humor forms (replicated, spontaneous, hybrid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate among replicated internet humor, spontaneous internet humor, and hybrid internet humor as distinct empirical categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replicated: content produced offline then uploaded; Spontaneous: created on the Net/designed for online (e.g., memes); Hybrid: mixes features of both (e.g., humorous YouTube film discussions). Use these distinctions to delimit data and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for interface-related constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how messaging applications and network design/interactional affordances pose cognitive or other challenges that shape the production and interpretation of internet humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 4 distinguishes interface-related constraints from user-related constraints; consider how platform affordances affect framing, multimodality, timing, and dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for user-related constraints (social identities, context collapse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how social identities (e.g., gender) and context collapse (heterogeneous imagined audiences) interfere with production and interpretation, including liberating and inhibiting effects for discriminatory humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 4 discusses social identity influence and context collapse (Marwick & Boyd 2011) as central to understanding online humor dissemination and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mixed methods: qualitative and quantitative analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine qualitative and quantitative approaches to study structural patterns and interpretative functions in online humor data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 5 illustrates this with WhatsApp data: qualitative analysis of laughter and emojis to signal humorous framing; quantitative analysis to reveal structural initiation patterns of humorous exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze multimodal resources (verbal + visual synergy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the synergy between verbal and visual resources (text + image + emoji) and their combined impact on interpretative complexity and humor resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 7 (memes) emphasizes interplay of verbal and visual resources; reviewer notes this synergy makes processing more complex and demands diverse inferential strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate inferential strategies and incongruity-resolution mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and describe diverse inferential strategies users employ to resolve incongruities in memetic and other internet humor, situating them within or alongside known logical mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RT-based inferential strategies are presented for meme interpretation; reviewer suggests more work comparing these strategies with established logical mechanisms (e.g., Attardo et al. 2002).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat cultural specificity and cross-cultural comparison carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat observed patterns as culture-specific rather than universal; include cross-cultural comparisons where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 5 includes a brief Spanish vs Chinese comparison, reminding readers that politeness norms and habits affect humor patterns; avoid overgeneralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine functions of paralinguistic and multimodal signals (laughter, emojis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze pragmatic functions of transcribed laughter and emojis in signaling humorous framing, intention, and interpretation among interlocutors with varying familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 5 focuses on how hahahaha and emojis operate pragmatically; use fine-grained transcript/annotation to capture these functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study social media humor practices and community dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate user activities on social media: uploading posts, creating archives/repositories, participating in groups for ingroup bonding/outgroup bounding, commenting, and polylogue structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 6 discusses forms humor takes on social networking sites, including corporate humor for engagement/profit and polylogues (mixed turn-taking and networked sequences). Compare with other scholars' findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider affective/non-propositional effects and identity construction
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to propositional/cognitive aspects, study non-propositional information and affect (construction of social identities, ingroup/outgroup dynamics, alleviation of negative feelings, encouragement to participate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 8 critiques RT's traditional focus on propositional content and urges expansion to cover affect and identity; reviewer signals importance of these effects for future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rich examples and detailed analyses afforded by monograph format
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide many examples and detailed analyses to illustrate interpretations and the semiotic features underlying claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer praises the monograph format for allowing detailed examples and analyses that clarify how the author works and the semiotic bases for interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly state limitations, open questions, and directions for future research
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize limitations of the approach and identify promising distinctions and unexplored research questions for younger scholars to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes the book lacks a concluding chapter summarizing limitations and future directions; recommends authors include explicit recapitulation of limitations and next steps (e.g., further exploration of partial/sustained/transitional/deferred relevance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore and empirically test subtle relevance-theoretic distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop and empirically examine nuanced RT concepts (partial, sustained, transitional, deferred relevance) through data analysis rather than leaving them largely theoretical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer finds these distinctions promising but insufficiently explored in data (pp. 113–114); encourages deeper empirical work on these types of relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situate findings within existing scholarship and provide comprehensive referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtapose findings with prior studies and provide useful references to situate contributions in the broader literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer highlights that Yus connects his findings with other scholars' studies and provides many references, which helps readers locate the work within existing research.
